_scope_definitions.all: Applies to every paper that reports a quantitative measure of anything. No trigger question; never NA.
_scope_definitions.external_comparison_validation: Does the paper state that it supports its measure by comparing it with something outside the measure itself — an official record, a criterion variable, an established alternative instrument, expert judgements, or a benchmark it names? Fires on that stated comparison-as-support. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting a correlation among its own items, or a descriptive correlation the paper does not offer as support for the measure. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.nomological_validation: Does the paper state that its measure is supported because it reproduces an expected, known, or theoretically predicted relationship with another variable? Fires on the paper offering that relationship as evidence for the measure. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting a substantive result that happens to match theory, without presenting it as validation of the measure. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.single_item_measure: Does the paper state that one question, one indicator, or one coded variable stands for a named concept in its analysis? Fires on the paper's own description of the operationalization (it names the concept and points to a single item). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a battery whose items are also reported separately, or a single variable that is a direct physical count rather than a stand-in for an abstract concept. Ambiguous cases are NA.
_scope_definitions.automated_text_measure: Does the paper state that a variable was produced from text by a computer procedure — counting words, classifying documents, fitting a topic or scaling model, applying a language model? Fires on the paper's own description of the procedure. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: people reading and coding the text by hand, or text used only as illustration. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.supervised_text_classifier: Does the paper state that it hand-labelled a set of documents and used them to train a procedure that then labelled the rest? Fires on that stated training-set-plus-classifier design. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a topic model or other procedure the paper describes as needing no labels, or a dictionary/word-list count. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.unsupervised_text_categories: Does the paper state that categories, topics, or clusters were discovered by a model rather than fixed in advance? Fires on the paper naming such a method or describing the categories as estimated from the data. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a classifier trained on a predefined scheme, or an exploratory factor analysis of survey items (not text). Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.dictionary_measure: Does the paper state that it scored text by counting words from a list, lexicon, dictionary, or keyword set? Fires on that self-description, whether the list is borrowed or purpose-built. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a trained classifier whose features happen to be words, or a hand-coding scheme that mentions keywords as guidance. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.text_scaling: Does the paper state that it placed actors, documents, or units on a latent dimension estimated from text — an ideology score, a position, a one-dimensional scale from word data? Fires on that self-description. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: classifying documents into categories, or scaling roll-call votes or survey items rather than text. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.latent_variable_model: Does the paper state that it fitted a measurement model with unobserved variables — factor analysis, structural equation model, item-response model, latent class or latent trait model? Fires on the paper naming such a model. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a principal-components summary the paper does not describe as a latent-variable model, random intercepts used as a nuisance term, or a simple index. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.fitted_measure_downstream: Does the paper state that a variable entering a subsequent analysis is the output of a model it fitted — factor scores, latent estimates, classifier predictions, topic proportions, or another model-produced value? Does NOT fire: a directly recorded variable; a simple sum or average of items (that fires sum_or_average_score); a published index used as given without the paper stating it fitted the model. Unclear whether the value came from a fitted model: NA.
_scope_definitions.alpha_reported: Does the paper report a coefficient alpha / Cronbach's alpha figure for a set of items? Fires on the reported number or the paper's statement that alpha was computed. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting inter-coder agreement, omega, composite reliability, or a test-retest correlation. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.sum_or_average_score: Does the paper state that the combined variable is a sum, total, count, or unweighted mean of its items? Fires only where the paper names that arithmetic. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a factor score, an item-response score, a weighted index, or a composite whose rule the paper never states (the unstated case is REPORT-08, not this). Ambiguous cases are NA.
_scope_definitions.established_instrument: Does the paper say it used an instrument that already exists — naming it, citing its source publication, or calling it established, standard, validated, or previously used? Near-miss that does NOT fire it: writing items the paper describes as its own, or reusing a variable from a public dataset without naming an instrument. Ambiguous cases are out of scope (NA), never FLAG.
_scope_definitions.mcmc_estimated: Fires when the paper states that its estimates come from a Markov chain Monte Carlo, Gibbs, Hamiltonian, or other posterior sampler. Near-miss: naming a Bayesian prior in a model fitted by optimisation does not fire it. Unclear how the model was fitted: NA.
_scope_definitions.multi_item_scale: Does the paper state that two or more items, indicators, or component sub-measures are combined into one variable it then analyses? Fires on the paper's own description of building a scale, index, factor score, or composite. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting several related variables side by side without combining them, or entering several indicators as separate regressors. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.unsupervised_text: Does the paper state that it used a procedure that discovers categories or dimensions from its texts without labels fixed in advance — a topic model, a clustering, an unsupervised scaling? Does NOT fire: a paper stating its categories were fixed in advance and applied by coders or a trained classifier. Unclear: NA.
_scope_definitions.conjunctive_construct: Does the paper state that its concept requires all of its named parts to be present together — that the parts are necessary conditions, defining attributes, or that a case lacking one does not have the concept? Fires only on that explicit statement about the concept's structure (see REPORT-15, which asks any paper combining several components to make the statement). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: listing several dimensions of a concept without saying whether they can substitute for one another. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.standardized_before_aggregation: Does the paper state that component variables were standardized, z-scored, normalized, or rescaled to a common range before being combined? Fires on the paper's own description of the rescaling step. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting standardized coefficients in a regression table, or reporting items that happen to share a response scale. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.ordinal_as_interval: Does the paper state that a variable it treats numerically is made of ranked or ordered categories — a rank, a graded classification, an ordinal index, a Likert item entered as a number? Fires on the paper's own description of the variable's categories. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a continuous measurement (money, counts, time) or a variable whose category structure the paper never describes. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.estimated_measure_downstream: Does the paper state that a variable entering its substantive analysis is itself an estimate produced by a model, a classifier, a scaling procedure, or a set of factor scores? Fires on the paper's own statement that the variable was estimated or predicted (see REPORT-02, which asks every paper to disclose which of its analysed values a model produced). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a directly recorded variable, or a simple sum of observed items. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.estimated_confounder: Fires when the paper states that a control variable in its analysis is such a model output. Near-miss: a recorded covariate, however imperfect, does not fire it. Unclear: NA.
_scope_definitions.declared_cutoff: Fires when the paper states that it applied a numeric cutoff to build its measure — a threshold for membership, for dichotomising, or for classifying. Near-miss: a conventional significance level, or a cutoff in a robustness appendix that does not produce the analysed measure, does not fire it. Unclear whether a cutoff produced the measure: NA.
_scope_definitions.reference_text_scaling: Does the paper state that the text scale's endpoints or reference points were set by designated anchor, training, or reference documents whose positions the analyst supplied? Fires on the paper naming those anchor documents. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a scaling model the paper describes as estimating positions without supplied anchors. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.cross_unit_latent_comparison: Does the paper state that it compares estimated latent scores across groups, periods, chambers, or item sets — for instance saying that units moved, that one group sits higher than another, or that scores from different periods are put on one scale? Fires on that stated comparison of estimated scores. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: reporting scores within a single group and period, or comparing directly observed variables. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.cross_context_measure: Does the paper state that one measurement instrument was applied across settings it describes as different — several countries, languages, historical periods, or distinct populations? Fires on the paper's own description of the spread of its cases. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a large sample drawn from one setting, or several settings measured with instruments the paper describes as separate and unconnected. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.administered_instrument: Does the paper state that it put questions, items, tasks, or stimuli to respondents or subjects and recorded their answers? Fires on the paper's own description of fielding an instrument (a survey battery, a questionnaire, an experimental task producing a recorded response). Near-miss that does NOT fire it: analysing an existing survey file, administrative records, or text produced for other purposes, without the paper saying it administered anything itself. If it is unclear whether the paper administered its own instrument, the trigger does not fire and every check gated on it is NA; a coder therefore never chooses between NA and FLAG for the same paper.
_scope_definitions.modified_instrument: Does the paper state that it changed an existing instrument — dropping, adding, or rewording items, altering response options, or rescoring it? Does NOT fire: administering a published instrument as originally specified; reporting a published instrument's own alternative short form as published. Unclear whether a change was made: NA.
_scope_definitions.new_instrument: Does the paper state that it created the measure itself — new items, a new coding scheme, a new index built for this study? Near-miss that does NOT fire it: adapting a named existing instrument (that is `established_instrument` plus REPORT-10), or assembling variables that already exist in a dataset. Ambiguity resolves out: NA, not FLAG.
_scope_definitions.human_coding: Does the paper state that people read, watched, or listened to material and assigned codes or categories to it for this study? Fires on the paper's own description of coders, coding, or content analysis. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: survey respondents answering about themselves, experts rating units on a scale (that is `expert_ratings`), or the paper using someone else's already-coded dataset without coding anything itself. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.supervised_classifier: Does the paper state that it trained a classifier or learner on cases it labelled by hand and applied it to unlabelled cases? Does NOT fire: a regression predicting a substantive outcome; applying a model built by someone else without stating that this paper trained one (that fires transported_instrument); a dictionary applied without training. Unclear: NA.
_scope_definitions.expert_or_coder_ratings: Fires when the paper states that the values it analyses were assigned by two or more human raters, coders, or experts judging units. Near-miss: a single author coding all cases alone, or survey respondents answering about themselves, does not fire it. Unclear how many people assigned the values: NA.
_scope_definitions.expert_ratings: Does the paper state that its values come from experts, judges, or raters scoring units on a response scale — either ratings it collected or a named expert-survey dataset? Fires on that self-description. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a single author coding cases, or coders applying a categorical codebook to documents (that is `human_coding`). Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.cross_validation_reported: Does the paper state that performance was estimated by cross-validation, repeated splitting, or a held-out fold procedure? Fires on that stated procedure. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: a single train/test split reported as such (that is covered by IDENT-10), or accuracy reported with no stated estimation procedure. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.
_scope_definitions.case_level_coding: Does the paper state that it assigned scores to a set of named cases (countries, parties, episodes, organizations) on the basis of case knowledge, historical or secondary sources? Fires on the paper's own description of case-by-case coding. Near-miss that does NOT fire it: coding a large sample of anonymous documents or respondents (that is `human_coding`), or importing a published country-year index without coding cases itself. Ambiguity resolves out to NA.

claim: The sources treat the bond between a paper's numbers and the idea they are said to stand for as a claim needing evidence a reader can inspect. No single assessment procedure settles that claim: each supplies one strand, a credible case pulls several together, and no amount of design or sample size repairs a measure that misses its target.
observable: How many distinct kinds of evidence the paper reports, or cites a named source as reporting, for the claim that its principal measured variable stands for the concept it is named after.
pass_condition: For its main measured construct the paper reports at least two distinct kinds from this list, or cites specific studies reporting them: a comparison of the measure against an outside record or criterion variable; a stated check of the instrument's content against the paper's own definition; agreement with a different instrument for the same concept; a test of an association the theory predicts; a fitted measurement model for the item set; human checking of machine-assigned values; re-examination of individual cases' scores against knowledge of those cases. Evidence in an appendix, supplement, footnote, or replication archive counts exactly as main-text evidence does.
flag_condition: The paper names a construct and analyses values for it while reporting fewer than two of the enumerated kinds anywhere and citing no source that reports them. claim: Agreement with a rival instrument counts in a measure's favour only where the paper gives a conceptual reason for expecting agreement; a bare correlation is not that argument, and for an instrument advertised as catching what others miss, close agreement counts against it.
observable: Whether the paper states a conceptual reason for expecting the agreement it reports with another instrument.

severity_basis: Adcock and Collier (2001) make a specific conceptual reason for expecting convergence a condition of counting agreement as evidence for validity, and note that for an indicator claimed to capture an overlooked facet close agreement is negative evidence; Seawright and Collier (2014) call bare-correlation convergence a practical and often insufficiently theorized check.
requirement_statement: A paper offering agreement with another instrument as validity evidence must state the conceptual grounds on which agreement was expected.

claim: A relationship assumed true in order to vouch for a measure cannot afterwards be presented as something that measure discovered; the study owes its readers a statement of which claims are now off-limits.
observable: Whether the relationship the paper used to vouch for its measure reappears among the paper's own reported findings.
pass_condition: The relationship invoked to support the measure is not also presented as a result of the paper; or the paper states explicitly that this relationship was assumed for validation and therefore is not offered as a finding.
flag_condition: The same relationship is used both as the ground for accepting the measure and as a substantive finding, with no statement that the two roles conflict.
severity_basis: Adcock and Collier (2001) hold that taking a causal claim for granted to vouch for a measure forecloses testing that same claim with it, and that the paper should say which later tests remain open.
requirement_statement: A paper must not report as a finding the same relationship it assumed in order to validate its measure.

claim: Standing one question in for a concept presupposes that the question and the concept move together almost exactly; for a many-sided topic that presupposition fails, and roughly half of a single item's variance is error even in well-run surveys.
observable: Whether the paper says anything about the error carried by the single item it uses for a named concept.

requirement_statement: A paper measuring a concept with one item must report that item's error or defend the single-item choice.

claim: No text model is a true account of language, so how a procedure behaves on one corpus says nothing about the next; the burden falls on the analyst to validate the measure in the application at hand, and producing numbers is not evidence that they refer to anything.
observable: Whether the paper reports a validation of its text-derived measure carried out on the corpus it actually analyses.
pass_condition: The paper reports a validation exercise performed on its own corpus — hand-checking a sample of the machine output, comparison with independently coded values for the same documents, or a stated comparison of the measure against known facts about those documents — and reports what that exercise found. Where the procedure is of a kind governed by IDENT-10, IDENT-11, IDENT-12, or IDENT-13, that more specific check carries the verdict and this one passes, so a single missing validation is recorded once rather than twice.
flag_condition: A text-derived variable is analysed with no validation on the paper's own corpus and none of IDENT-10 to IDENT-13 applies to the procedure used; or the measure is supported only by citing the method's performance elsewhere.
severity_basis: Grimmer and Stewart (2013) state that running a text method and reporting its output with no validation is not acceptable practice, and that evidence a method worked on one corpus does not license assuming it works on another.
requirement_statement: A paper using an automated text measure must report a validation of that measure on its own corpus.

claim: A measure built by reading texts must state the interpretive setting in which the reading was done, since the same passage supports several legitimate readings.
observable: A passage setting out the frame the analysis works in: who produced the texts, for what audience, and what the analyst takes the language to be evidence about.

flag_condition: The paper reports text-derived values with no passage stating the frame in which the texts were read.
severity_basis: Krippendorff holds that replication is impossible when readers cannot tell which frame produced the results, and that no text-based measurement can proceed before that frame is fixed.
requirement_statement: A paper measuring from text states the interpretive setting in which its texts were read.

claim: A classifier trained on a fixed scheme is judged by putting its labels beside human labels for the same documents; the documents used for that comparison must be ones the fitted model never saw, and the comparison has to be broken out by category, because the share of a category's documents the machine finds and the share of its assignments that are right diverge and expose different failures.
observable: Whether the paper reports the classifier's agreement with human labels on documents held out of fitting, and whether that performance is broken out by category.
pass_condition: The paper reports a comparison of machine labels against human labels on documents it states were not used in fitting or tuning the model — through a held-out set or a cross-validation procedure — and reports that comparison category by category: a cross-tabulation of human against machine labels, or per-category figures covering both the share of a category's documents the classifier found and the share of its assignments to that category that were right.
flag_condition: No comparison with human labels is reported; or figures are reported with no statement that they come from documents withheld from fitting, so a reader cannot tell whether the model was scored on its own training data; or only an overall accuracy or agreement figure is reported; or per-category figures are given for only one of the two directions of error. claim: Categories a model discovers carry no guarantee of bearing on the concept the study cares about, and any single clustering is partly an artefact of the model that produced it; the categories, and anything aggregated out of them, have to be validated before substantive use.
observable: Whether the paper reports a validation of its discovered categories, and of any quantity built from them, before drawing substantive conclusions.
pass_condition: The paper reports at least one validation of the estimated categories performed on its own corpus — human judgement of whether documents within a category belong together and are separable from other categories, hand-coding a sample under the discovered scheme and checking agreement, or lining up movements in a category's measured attention against events known independently — and reports validation for any derived quantity it analyses.

requirement_statement: A paper using model-discovered categories must validate them, and anything derived from them, on its own corpus before substantive use.
